{{nihongo|'''Han-style mirror'''|漢鏡|Kankyou|Hàn jìng}}) refers to a general term for {{ill|Bronze mirror|en|Bronze mirror|qid=Q1041984|lt=bronze mirrors}} produced during the Chinese {{ill|Han BCE–220 CE). Most were made of {{ill|Cupronickel|en|Cupronickel|qid=Q649090|lt=Cupronickel}}, {{Refnest|group=note|In modern times, white bronze is defined as an alloy of [[copper]] and [[nickel]]. However, prior to this, white bronze referred to a type of {{ill|Bronze|en|Bronze|qid=Q34095|lt=bronze}} with a particularly high tin content of 25–30%. This definition is still often used in historical disciplines like {{ill|Archaeology|en|Archaeology|qid=Q23498|lt=archaeology}}. As the tin content in bronze increases, its color shifts from a reddish hue, like that of a {{ill|10 yen coin|ja|10円硬貨|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 十円硬貨|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q4546963}}, to a silvery-white, while also becoming harder and more brittle.{{sfn|Tanabe Yoshikazu|1971|p=445}}}} and were primarily used as {{ill|Makeup|ja|化粧|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q1190910}}.  

The mirrors were predominantly circular. Early Han mirrors often featured flat surfaces, but convex mirrors became more prevalent in later periods. The reverse side of the mirrors (the side opposite the reflective surface) was often adorned with patterns and inscriptions reflecting the cosmological and {{ill|Xian (Taoism)|ja|神仙思想|lt=immortality beliefs|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 仙人|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q1207451}} of the time. {{Refnest|group=note|Immortality beliefs involved the faith in the existence of {{ill|Xian (Taoism)|en|Xian (Taoism)|qid=Q1207451|lt=immortals}} and the aspiration to become immortal through specific practices.{{sfn|Kotobank: Immortality Beliefs}}}} These patterns and inscriptions, along with their classifications into "mirror styles," are valuable in {{ill|Absolute dating|en|Absolute dating|qid=Q332423|lt=archaeological dating}} for estimating the periods of relics and ruins. Mirrors with inscriptions bearing {{ill|Era name|ja|元号|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q256408}}, known as "dated inscription mirrors" (紀年銘鏡), are particularly significant for chronological studies. Additionally, the study of the imagery and inscriptions on Kan mirrors is of great interest in Chinese {{ill|Intellectual history|en|Intellectual_history|qid=Q1195695|lt=intellectual history}} and {{ill|History of literature|en|History_of_literature|qid=Q6497044|lt=literary history}}.{{sfn|Okamura Hidenori|1984|p=661}}{{sfn|Okamura Hidenori|2017|p=44-46}}  

Kan mirrors, thought to have been gifted by the Han court to tributary states as reciprocal gifts, have been unearthed across a wide area of East Asia, including the {{ill|Japanese archipelago|en|Japanese archipelago|qid=Q841337|lt=Japanese archipelago}}, {{ill|Korean Peninsula|ja|朝鮮半島|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q483134}}, {{ill|Vietnam|en|Vietnam|qid=Q881|lt=Vietnam}}, and {{ill|Central Asia|en|Central Asia|qid=Q27275|lt=Central Asia}}.{{sfn|Morishita Akihiko|2019|p=13}} This distribution reflects the extent of the Han dynasty's interaction network. {{Refnest|group=note|The westernmost site where Kan mirrors have been found is the Tillya Tepe archaeological site in {{ill|Afghanistan|en|Afghanistan|qid=Q889|lt=Afghanistan}}.{{sfn|Morishita Akihiko|2019|p=25-28}}}} In the Japanese archipelago, Kan mirrors were likely introduced through {{ill|Lelang Commandery|en|Lelang Commandery|qid=Q701376|lt=Lelang Commandery}} on the Korean Peninsula and are found in sites dating from the {{ill|Yayoi period|en|Yayoi period|qid=Q207858|lt=Yayoi period}} to the early {{ill|Kofun period|en|Kofun period|qid=Q459939|lt=Kofun period}}. While many were interred as {{ill|Grave goods|en|Grave goods|qid=Q1399692|lt=grave goods}} for prominent individuals, they have also been excavated from settlement and {{ill|ritual sites|ja|祭祀遺跡|qid=Q109358391}}. These mirrors are believed to have been used as {{ill|prestige goods|ja|威信財}} or {{ill|amulets|ja|呪具}}.{{sfn|Tsujita Junichirō|2019|p=8-9}}{{sfn|Morishita Akihiko|2019|p=19-20}}  

Even after the fall of the Han dynasty, imitation Kan mirrors continued to be produced, influencing later bronze mirrors. The term '''Kan-style mirrors''' (漢式鏡) broadly encompasses mirrors bearing the characteristics of Kan mirrors without restricting the time or place of production, and this article also touches on these.{{sfn|Kotobank: Kan-style mirrors}}
